boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's siege and capture of Amantea (18 December 1806 to 6 February 1807 by Bodart) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1806 group: Huard's investment of the 18th [December] by Koch, the siege works and assaults, the mine and the capitulation of 6 February. Verdier's blockade after Maida, his failed first attempt of 3 to 8 December, the risings round Cosenza and Lamarque's siege of Maratea are context. Side A is the French. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) 4,700 men under General of Division Reynier and side B (the Neapolitan garrison) about 1,300 men under Colonel Mirabelli. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. His 4,700 equals Koch's three bodies sent against the place, Huard's 1,200, Verdier's 2,500 and Reynier's 1,000 (our arithmetic; claim koch-side-a). The passages read give no number for the garrison: Koch describes regular troops, some hundreds of insurgents and the inhabitants, and Colletta few soldiers and many Bourbon partisans (claims koch-side-b and colletta-side-b). The one 1,300 in the passages read for Amantea is Koch's strength of Verdier's column for the first attempt of 3 December (claim koch-side-a), and they do not show where Bodart's figure comes from. Koch has the besiegers sent in execution of the marshal's orders, and the garrison held the place before the siege, so the claim is tagged inherited. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'the French (4,700 men) under General of Division Reynier force the Neapolitan garrison (about 1,300 men) under Colonel Mirabelli to surrender'. 'Div.-Gen.' is Divisions-General in Bodart's list of abbreviations.

claims.value: Side A (French), its own account in Koch: in execution of the orders the marshal gave after settling at Cosenza on 15 December the final dispositions for the attack, a corps of 1,200 men under Colonel Huard, acting as general of brigade, invested the fortress on the 18th; Verdier set out on the 22nd with 2,500 men and 6 pieces of ordnance and was followed the next day by a column of 1,000 men brought by General Reynier. Before Bodart's dates, Verdier had left Cosenza on 3 December for the first attempt with 1,300 men, 2 howitzers and 2 mountain pieces.
claims.rationale: Side A's history, read from the page images. Koch's three bodies make 4,700 (our arithmetic), Bodart's figure (claim bodart-strength); the passages read give no single strength for the force before the place on one day and no count of its losses or reinforcements during the siege. Koch gives the day of the investment as 'the 18th' without a month, in a narrative that has just brought the marshal to Cosenza on 15 December; read as 18 December, it is Bodart's first date. The page image of p. 282 is heavily inked, and the transcription reads the first figure of '22' by its shape. Koch's 'his orders' follow the marshal's instructions to Reynier, and the force moved in execution of them, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'meanwhile it had to be finished: the marshal went on 15 December to Cosenza, where he settled the final dispositions concerning the attack on Amantea' (p. 281); 'in execution of his orders, a corps of 1,200 men led by Colonel Huard, performing the' (p. 281) 'functions of general of brigade, formed the investment of the fortress on the 18th. Verdier set out on the 22nd with 2,500 men and 6 pieces of ordnance; he was followed the next day by a column of 1,000 men brought by General Reynier, who directed all the operations of the siege' (p. 282); 'reassured on this point, Verdier, in accordance with the marshal's orders, left Cosenza on 3 December to reduce Amantea, at the head of 1,300 men, 2 howitzers and 2 mountain pieces' (p. 280).

claims.value: Side A's command and decisions. Koch: after Maida, General Verdier, charged with the command of Calabria Citeriore, held its capital and kept Amantea blockaded until bands threatened to surround him and he recalled the blockade corps (OCR). Masséna would have scrupled to leave Cosenza without reducing Amantea and Maratea, and he charged Verdier with taking Amantea and General Lamarque with taking Maratea (OCR). In accordance with the marshal's orders Verdier left Cosenza on 3 December with 1,300 men, 2 howitzers and 2 mountain pieces; before the place a first escalade of the bastioned front failed, and a second, some days later, between the rocks facing the sea while the bastioned front was attacked by force, failed too; these two failures, the consumption of food and munitions and the 3,000 insurgents established between Lagonegro and Amantea decided him to withdraw on 8 December. The marshal went to Cosenza on 15 December, settled the final dispositions for the attack on Amantea and left for Naples on the 21st, having first instructed General Reynier, to whom the command fell by right, to distribute his troops in brigades camped at Cosenza, Catanzaro and Monteleone, to form mobile columns pursuing the bands, to garrison the posts as they surrendered and to keep the column chiefs in touch with the authorities. In execution of his orders Colonel Huard, acting as general of brigade, invested the fortress on the 18th; Verdier set out on the 22nd and Reynier followed the next day and directed all the operations of the siege; Reynier granted the garrison leave to pass to Sicily. Colletta: General Verdier went to assault the place; having invested the front of the castle toward the country and raised a battery, he sent his bravest soldiers forward with the ladders at first light, but they were driven back; after other attacks had failed, on a long dark December night a party of seven climbed the rocks between the town and the sea while a larger column followed with ropes and ladders and other troops attacked the bastioned wall to divert the defenders, but a child's cry from the sea front raised the alarm, one of the seven was killed, a howitzer [shell] bursting in the air showed the assailants and many French were killed; the general raised the siege and returned to Cosenza. When December was over he came back to the assaults, bringing Colonel Amato, also a citizen of Amantea and Mirabelli's kinsman and childhood companion and friend, who wrote to Mirabelli on reaching the camp.
claims.rationale: Side A's chain of command as Koch and Colletta give it (page images except the passages marked OCR). Bodart and Koch credit Reynier with the siege; Colletta has Verdier conduct both the first attack and the siege and does not name Reynier, so the commander at the siege is disputed. In Koch Verdier commanded Calabria Citeriore (OCR), led the first attempt and brought the largest column to the siege. Colletta's 'he' who came back when December was over refers to 'the general', Verdier, of the preceding sentences. Colletta's night attempt on the sea side, with a diversion against the bastioned wall, matches in its description Koch's second escalade between the rocks facing the sea while the bastioned front was attacked; both precede Verdier's withdrawal. The decisions described are side A's commanders', the marshal's included, so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): Koch, 'General Verdier, charged with the command of Calabria Citeriore'; 'and kept Amantea blockaded by'; 'Verdier at once recalled the blockade corps' (OCR); 'Masséna would have made it a scruple to leave Cosenza before having reduced them. He charged General Verdier with carrying the latter, and General Lamarque with taking the other' (OCR); as in claim koch-side-a for the first departure (p. 280); 'arrived before this' (p. 280) 'place, Verdier attempted on the bastioned front a first escalade, which failed. A second, tried some days later between the rocks that face the sea while the bastioned front was attacked by force, was equally unsuccessful. These two failures, the consumption of the food and munitions, and moreover the anxiety that 3,000 insurgents who had established themselves between Lagonegro and Amantea gave Verdier, decided him to withdraw on 8 December'; as in claim koch-side-a for the final dispositions; 'there he renewed to the king the pressing request for a leave, which was at last granted him, and left for Naples on the 21st. Beforehand he had instructed General Reynier, to whom the command fell by right, to distribute his troops in roughly equal brigades and to have them camp at Cosenza, Catanzaro and Monteleone; to have the generals form mobile columns of a third of their forces, which would be continually on the move and would range round these three points, pursuing without respite all the bands that might be landed on the coast; to put garrisons in the posts as they surrendered, provisioning them for a month or six weeks; finally to require that the chiefs of these mobile columns be in direct relation with the constituted authorities, so as to be warned in time of all these insurrectionary movements' (p. 281); as in claim koch-side-a for the investment and the siege (pp. 281-282); 'Reynier granted the garrison leave to pass to Sicily, on condition of not serving against us for a year and a day' (p. 282); Colletta, as in claim colletta-side-a for the first attack; 'and then, having surrounded that front of the castle that faces the country and raised a battery of cannon and howitzers, at the first light of day, at an agreed signal, the bravest soldiers advanced at the run with the ladders; but the strength of the place and the valour of the garrison drove them back, so that, reduced, they returned to the camps. Other attacks, other assaults, other threats having come to nothing'; 'on a long dark night of December, a small party of seven men, the most nimble first, climbing among the rocks that separate the town from the sea'; 'while a larger column with ropes and ladders silently followed the marked tracks, and other troops, shouting and firing, attacked the bastioned wall to divert the defenders from the true assault. But at a child's voice crying "the French" from the sea front, the guards run up'; 'one of the seven is hit and dies'; 'when a howitzer [shell] from the camp burst in the air and by its light revealed the assailants'; 'many of the French were killed, the others halted and gathered in the camps. The general, when he saw that neither surprises, nor tricks, nor force sufficed, raised the siege and returned, grieving and thirsting for revenge, to Cosenza'; 'but when December was over, he, stronger, better provided with engines, returned to the assaults, bringing on his side Colonel Amato, also a citizen of Amantea, kinsman and from childhood companion and friend of Mirabelli' (p. 32); 'to whom, on arriving at the camp, he wrote affectionately' (p. 33).

claims.value: Bodart records that side A (French) under Reynier forced the Neapolitan garrison to surrender, dating the siege from 18 December 1806 to 6 February 1807; the garrison was allowed to march out with all the honours of war and, against the obligation not to serve against France or its allies for a year, to embark for Sicily. Koch: several assaults were repulsed and the besiegers had to mine, and only on 6 February, after 33 days of siege, did the place capitulate; Reynier granted the garrison leave to pass to Sicily on condition of not serving against the French for a year and a day. Colletta: the two besieged castles, Amantea and Cotrone, yielded at last, their garrisons with different fates but equal glory; hunger alone made the castle of Amantea surrender, on honourable terms, after forty days of siege, not counting the first assault, and the garrisons returned to Sicily as prisoners for a year and a day.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome (side A won), read from Bodart's entry, with the other accounts' ending (page images). The accounts agree on the surrender and the garrison's passage to Sicily. Bodart's year against Koch's and Colletta's year and a day is a difference in the reported terms; Bodart's honours of war are not in the passages read, where Colletta has honourable terms and Koch the passage to Sicily only. Colletta puts the surrender down to hunger alone; Koch gives no reason beyond the siege works and the mine. Bodart's first date is the day of Huard's investment in Koch (claim koch-side-a); Koch counts 33 days of siege and Colletta forty, without the first assault, and the passages read do not say from what day either counts. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength, and '1806 18/12 to 1807 6/2. siege and capture of Amantea'; 'the garrison was allowed to march out with all the honours of war and, against the obligation not to serve against France or its allies for one year, to embark for Sicily'; Koch, 'several assaults having been repulsed, it was necessary to go underground, and it was only on 6 February, after 33 days of siege, that the place capitulated' (p. 282), and as in claim side-a-command for the terms; Colletta, 'Massena, after having laid siege to Amantea and Cotrone, on reaching Palme, stopped'; 'the two besieged castles yielded at last, with different fates for the garrisons but equal glory' (p. 31); 'but hunger hung over the Calabrians, and for it alone the little castle of Amantea, armed with three corroded cannon, defended by inexperienced partisans, assailed by very strong forces with the best arts of war, after forty days of siege (without counting the first assault) surrendered on honourable terms. The garrisons returned to Sicily as prisoners for a year and a day' (p. 33).

claims.value: Bodart places Amantea, a town in southern Italy, Calabria, on the Tyrrhenian Sea, 23 km southwest of Cosenza. Koch: the town is built on a rock near the sea, 30 kilometres south-west of Cosenza, with an enceinte of roughly square form, sheltered on three sides by the escarpment of the rocks on which it rests and closed on the fourth by an old bastioned front; it was scarcely safe from a coup de main, but the insurrection had given it importance because one could come up to it by boat from the sea. claims.value: Side A brought siege artillery and mined; in Colletta hunger forced side B's surrender. Koch: Verdier set out with 2,500 men and 6 pieces of ordnance; a trench was opened 260 metres from the place and pushed to 40 metres from the capital of the right bastion, where a battery of 6 pieces brought down the escarp after 48 hours of fire; after several assaults were repulsed the besiegers had to mine. The place could be reached by boat from the sea. In the first attempt, before Bodart's dates, the consumption of food and munitions was one of the reasons for Verdier's withdrawal. Colletta: before the first attack the place's munitions and victuals sufficed; Verdier came back better provided with engines; several batteries were raised against the castle, the breach was opened after some days of fire, and a bastion was mined and blown; hunger hung over the Calabrians, and for it alone the castle surrendered.
claims.rationale: Means and supply as the passages read give them (page images). No supply return was inspected, and the passages read do not say whether the place was supplied from the sea during the siege or how its food ran short. The transcription reads the first figure of '48' on the heavily inked p. 282 by its shape. Side A's means were set by the marshal's dispositions and the direction of the siege, and side B's by its own stores, so the claim is tagged unresolved. English renderings (ours): Koch, as in claims koch-side-a and amantea-ground; 'a trench boyau was opened 260 metres from the place and pushed to 40 metres from the capital of the right bastion, where a battery of 6 pieces was established, which brought down the escarp after 48 hours of fire' (p. 282); as in claim bodart-winner for the mining (p. 282) and claim side-a-command for the withdrawal (p. 281); Colletta, as in claims colletta-side-b and colletta-side-a; as in claim side-b-command for the batteries and the mine (p. 33); as in claim bodart-winner for the hunger (p. 33).

claims.value: Both sides fought from works. Side B held a walled town: Koch gives it an enceinte of roughly square form, sheltered on three sides by the escarpment of its rocks and closed on the fourth by an old bastioned front, scarcely safe from a coup de main; Colletta closes it on three sides by cliffs and on the fourth by an old wall between two weak bastions, calls it a castle whose bastions were armed with three iron cannon, and has other, newly built fortifications bar the passage when a mined bastion fell. Side A fought from siege works: Koch has a trench pushed to 40 metres from the capital of the right bastion, where a battery of 6 pieces brought down the escarp, and a mine; Colletta has several batteries raised against the castle and a bastion mined.
claims.rationale: Code both_fortified, as for Gaëta (B371a): side B defended permanent walls and bastions and new works behind the breach, and side A's battery fought from its trench (Koch) and its batteries against the castle (Colletta). The old walls are permanent (inherited); the new works were built during the siege, and the passages read do not say on whose order; side A's trench and batteries were built for this siege, which Reynier directed (Koch); one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. A coding that counted only the defended position would give B_fortified. The accounts agree on the code, so they are one claim. English renderings (ours): Koch, as in claims amantea-ground, means-and-supply and bodart-winner; Colletta, as in claims amantea-ground, colletta-side-b and side-b-command.

open_questions: Deferred: Koch refers to pièce justificative n° XIII for the first attempt; the parent OCR's pièces include Verdier's report on that attempt, under a heading the OCR does not give as n° XIII, with figures for his force, the insurgents and his loss that the OCR does not read as Koch's text does and with his intention to return before the place; the pièce lies outside the selection, its page image is not registered, and it is not cited and its figures are not restated. Also deferred: the parent OCR's account of an earlier combined operation against Amantea, given up when Reynier did not join Verdier, and of an English squadron anchored before the place (outside the selection; not cited); the articles of the capitulation, which the passages read do not print; Neapolitan, Sicilian and British accounts of the defence, none inspected.

Most consequential gap: side B's strength. Bodart gives the garrison about 1,300 men; Koch describes regular troops, some hundreds of insurgents and the inhabitants, and Colletta few soldiers and many Bourbon partisans, with no number in either. The targeted follow-up searched the whole parent OCR of Koch's volume for Amantea and Mirabelli and found no strength for the garrison; besides the passages above it found Koch's remark, in his opening description of the kingdom, that Brindisi, Otranto, Scilla, Amantea and others cannot be called fortresses but only simple coast batteries (outside the selection; not cited). A Neapolitan or British return of the garrison could narrow the gap.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side A's commander at the siege (Bodart and Koch Reynier; Colletta Verdier); side B's guns (Koch 4 to 5 pieces; Colletta three iron cannon); the distance from Cosenza (Bodart 23 km; Koch 30 kilometres); the length of the siege (Koch 33 days; Colletta forty, without the first assault; Bodart 18 December to 6 February); the parole (Bodart a year; Koch and Colletta a year and a day); the honours of war (Bodart; Colletta honourable terms; Koch neither); the cause of the surrender (Colletta hunger alone; Koch none given beyond the mine); and, before Bodart's dates, the strength of the first attempt (Koch 1,300 men; Colletta three thousand two hundred).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his 4,700 equals Koch's three bodies by our arithmetic, but the passages read do not show what he used, and his 1,300 and 500 are not in them); Koch (the French history of 1850 from Masséna's papers and the war depot; second-hand for the garrison); Colletta (the Neapolitan history by a Neapolitan officer, printed in this edition in 1856; the passages read give him no role at Amantea and name no source). No passage read shows dependence between Koch and Colletta.
